stops.name: Iconium, the window, and the voice of Paul
stops.campa: In Onesiphorus's house at Iconium the apostle Paul preaches continence and the resurrection to come, and a girl of the city, betrothed to the nobleman Thamyris, sits at the window across the street and does not move for three days and nights, neither to eat nor to rise, fastened to the sill by the word alone. Her mother Theocleia calls to her and she does not answer. This is Thecla, pearl not yet named pearl, and the voice she hears through the window is the first of the three waters this life will be baptized in.

stops.name: Iconium, the stake in the theater, and the storm
stops.campa: Thamyris and Theocleia denounce her to the governor, who condemns her to burn rather than let a word from a stranger cost him a bride-price. In the theater the wood is stacked and lit; Thecla makes the sign of the cross over the pyre and steps in unafraid, as into a bridal chamber. God sends a cloud heavy with rain and hail; the fire hisses out under the downpour, and the crowd that came to watch her die watches instead a girl escape a fire that will not touch her, and slip ungrieved into the press toward the road Paul has taken.

stops.name: Antioch, Alexander's assault in the street
stops.campa: Following Paul out of Iconium she comes to Antioch, and there a leading citizen named Alexander, struck by her beauty, seizes her in the open street meaning to have her. Thecla tears his cloak away and knocks the garland from his head, shaming a magistrate of Rome before the whole marketplace. Alexander drags her before the governor for the insult rather than confess the assault, and the city, delighted by the spectacle of a girl who fights back, condemns her to the wild beasts, to die for a violence she only refused.

stops.name: Antioch, the arena, the seals, and the self-baptism
stops.campa: In the amphitheater a lioness set to kill her instead lies at her feet and dies defending her from a bear and a lion. Queen Tryphaena, mourning her own dead daughter, has taken Thecla for her own and faints at the sight, staying the games for grief. Last, Thecla is thrown into a moat of man-eating seals: she flings herself in first, crying that she baptizes herself in the name of Jesus Christ on this, her last day. Lightning splits the water, and the seals float up dead all around her, unharmed.
stops.quote: In the name of Jesus Christ do I baptize myself on the last day.
stops.quote_source: Acts of Paul and Thecla, 34 (2nd c. apocryphon)

stops.name: Iconium, the return, and the mother who will not open the door
stops.campa: Freed by the governor at Tryphaena's plea, Thecla cuts her hair, puts on a man's tunic, and finds Paul again to be sent out to teach in his name. She returns once more to Iconium hoping to bring her mother Theocleia to the faith that has cost her a stake and an arena; her mother will not receive her. Thecla leaves the house of her childhood a last time, wearing a man's clothes, carrying no dowry but two deaths refused, and turns south toward the mountain city of Seleucia.

stops.name: Seleucia, the cave, the long teaching, and the earth that opens
stops.campa: For decades Thecla lives in a cave above Seleucia, teaching, healing the sick who climb to her, and converting the daughters of the pagan city, until physicians jealous of a healer who takes no fee send men to violate her old age. She prays, and the rock face of the mountain opens and receives her living body into itself, leaving her enemies clutching a torn piece of her veil. The tradition keeps her not as a grave but as a door in stone: the first runaway of this book to become, instead of a body, a threshold.

stops.name: Antioch, birth, and the death of the mother
stops.campa: Margaret is born in Antioch on the Orontes in the year 291, daughter of the pagan priest the canon calls Theodosius and, in another hand, Aedesius: the record keeps both names honestly, as it keeps her under two others still to come. Her mother dies soon after the birth, and the infant is given to a nurse to raise outside the city, a woman who is, unknown to the priest, a Christian in secret. The girl who will be called pearl begins her life carried already between a father's temple and a nurse's hidden altar.

stops.name: Antioch, the nurse's sheep, and the conversion of a child
stops.campa: Raised outside Antioch's walls, Margaret tends her nurse's sheep on the hillside and is taught the faith her father would kill her for, and takes to it entire, as a child takes to a story that turns out to be true. When Theodosius learns his daughter has been baptized in secret he disowns her outright. She keeps the sheep and keeps the faith both, unhoused by her father's roof but sheltered, she says later, by a greater one: the first exile of every timeline this one life will carry.

stops.name: Antioch, Olybrius, the refusal, the rods
stops.campa: At fifteen, keeping the flock by the road, Margaret is seen by Olybrius, the Roman diocese of the East, who wants her for wife or concubine and sends for her. She tells him plainly she is a Christian and will have no husband but Christ. He has her beaten bloody with rods in the public street and thrown into a cell to break her overnight, certain a shepherd girl's faith will not survive till morning. It is the oldest bargain offered to every runaway bride in this family: recant and marry, or keep the name and be broken.
stops.quote: O what shame is it to you, when you read the pain of Christ and the glory, and believe one thing and deny another.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend (Caxton translation, 1483), Life of Saint Margaret

stops.name: Antioch, the cell, the dragon, the cross that opens it
stops.campa: In the dark of the cell Margaret prays God to show her the enemy she fights in the flesh, that faith not remain a thing only spoken. Satan answers by becoming a serpent-dragon of enormous size, opens its jaws, and swallows her whole. Inside the belly of the beast she does not despair; she makes the sign of the cross with her bound hands, and the cross, growing in the dark gullet, bursts the dragon open and sets her free unmarked. A second devil appears in another shape at once; she throws him down and sets her foot on his neck.
stops.quote: Lie still, thou fiend, under the feet of a woman.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend (Caxton, 1483), Life of Saint Margaret

stops.name: Antioch, the public square, fire and iron, the rope
stops.campa: Brought again before Olybrius and the crowd, Margaret refuses the gods of Rome a second time, in daylight, before witnesses who cannot later claim they were not there. The authorities burn her with torches, tear her sides with iron combs, and bind her with rope to drag her through the square: a public unmaking meant to be watched to its end, so no one converted by rumor could later doubt it happened. She endures it singing, the Legend says, and the crowd that came to see a girl broken begins instead to weep.
stops.quote: Christ gave Himself over to the death for me, and I desire gladly to die for Christ.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend (Caxton, 1483), Life of Saint Margaret

stops.name: Antioch, the sealed vessel, the coronal event, the beheading
stops.campa: Last, they seal Margaret into a great vessel of water to drown her where fire and iron have failed. At the moment of her sealing the sky over Antioch opens with thunder, and a plasma crown descends and forms itself around her head, visible over the whole square; thousands of the watching crowd convert on the spot, undone by the light more than by the argument. Olybrius, seeing his own authority burn away with every witness, orders her beheading before the conversions can spread further, and it is done outside the walls that same hour.
stops.quote: Father Almighty, I yield to you thankings that You have suffered me to come to this glory, beseeching You to pardon them that pursue me... if any woman with child travailing in any place, call on me, that thou wilt keep her from peril, and that the child may be delivered from her belly without any hurt of his members.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend (Caxton, 1483), Life of Saint Margaret
